catalog_quote: [p.47] The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High ... and Low ..., which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling ..., and less frequently, Rising ... tones. Faraclas (1984a,b) argues that for Obolo, there is a third contrastive tone, which he calls Extra-high. In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.55] Unfortunately, Ward's discussion of stress does not go any deeper than suggesting stress is related to verb stems, and in fact, it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward. [fn.32, p.55] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress. [fn.34, p.56] ... as the foot is a notion usually associated with stress phenomena, it is by no means clear how it would apply in a non-stress language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for all Lower Cross languages (Connell's first-hand sample explicitly includes Ibino): two level tones (H, L) plus contrastive downstep, i.e. terraced-level tone languages; no evidence for word-level (lexical/root) stress -- LC treated as 'non-stress' languages -- though some phrasal stress and stress marking of compound junctures probably exist. No syllable position is designated as stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Ward's (1933) claim of verb-root stress in Efik is discussed and rejected; Faraclas (1984b) analyses Obolo with phrasal stress and an extra-high tone; Ibibio positional consonant weakening 'may be related to stress.. which to date remains unstudied' (p.104). None of these concern Ibino specifically.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about the Lower Cross group as a whole, argued mainly from Efik/Ibibio; word-level stress is denied, phrase-level stress is conjectured (uninvestigated except Obolo). Citation-form lexical items are the basis of the tonal claim (p.47). No Ibino-specific prosodic description exists in the thesis.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is group-level for the Lower Cross languages, not Ibino-specific; Connell's first-hand sample explicitly includes Ibino (= Ibeno/Ibuno, Akwa Ibom; glottocode ibin1241, ISO ibn; Wikipedia now titles it 'Ibono'). His prosodic argumentation draws mainly on Efik (efik1245), Ibibio (ibib1240) and, via Faraclas, Obolo (obol1243). No dialect of Ibino is distinguished.
